patient.name: Yusuf Ahmed
patient.complaint: Five days of fever, cough and red eyes, now a spreading rash
background: Attends nursery in Tower Hamlets; a classmate had a rash last week
Older sister Aaliyah, 8, has sickle cell disease

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a child who has fever then rash: the timing of the rash against the fever and one signature sign (Koplik spots, slapped cheeks, strawberry tongue, palms and soles) decides the answer.

points: Days 1 to 3: high fever, **cough, runny nose, red sticky eyes**.
Day 4: a blotchy rash started **behind his ears**.
Now spreading down to his face and trunk.

steps.lead: Yusuf has a widespread rash with fever, malaise and URTI symptoms in childhood: a **viral exanthem**. The job is to name which one.
Fever first, then a **maculopapular** rash, in a child with an infected nursery contact: Yusuf follows the usual pattern.

points: Inside his cheeks: tiny **white spots** on a red base.
Rash is red, blotchy and **maculopapular**, merging in places.
No strawberry tongue; palms and soles clear.

steps.q: White spots on Yusuf's buccal mucosa after cough, coryza and conjunctivitis point to which exanthem?
steps.r: **Koplik spots** after the three Cs (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis) are pathognomonic of **measles**.

steps.lead: Yusuf's three Cs, **Koplik spots** and a rash spreading down from **behind the ears** on day 4 is classic measles. Learn the other six signatures alongside it.

steps.title: Which exanthem? The signature clues
head: Exanthem
Cause
Signature clue
rows: 3 Cs, **Koplik spots**, rash from behind ears
3 days high fever, **rash as fever settles**
Vesicles at different stages, torso and face

visual.title: Fever and rash timing: measles vs roseola
visual.caption: In measles the rash arrives at the height of the fever; in roseola the rash appears as the fever settles.

steps.lead: Most exanthems are fever then rash, so for Yusuf it is the **Koplik spots** and the rash's spread from behind the ears that decide it.
Yusuf has measles' **commonest complication, otitis media**. Watch his breathing: **pneumonia** is the commonest cause of measles death.

steps.text: **Scarlet fever** is bacterial (Group A Strep), not viral, but is examined with the exanthems. A sandpaper rash plus strawberry tongue needs **antibiotics**, unlike the viral rashes.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' where the answer is usually none (clinical diagnosis); viral PCR is the answer only when the child is severely unwell or the diagnosis must be confirmed.

steps.r: Viral exanthems are **clinical diagnoses**: fever plus rash plus the signature features.

steps.lead: Yusuf's three Cs, Koplik spots and rash pattern make the diagnosis without a test.

points: Yusuf is admitted: dehydrated, breathing fast, SpO2 94%.
Measles is **notifiable**: the team must confirm it.

steps.lead: Yusuf is now **severely unwell**, so bloods and **viral PCR** (oral fluid or throat swab) confirm the organism.

steps.title: Yusuf's results
steps.text: Measles PCR positive with **lymphopenia**, reflecting the transient immune suppression measles causes.
Do not pick 'blood cultures' or 'skin biopsy' to diagnose a typical exanthem. **Clinical** is the answer; **PCR** only if severe.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?': supportive care for viral rashes, phenoxymethylpenicillin for scarlet fever, flucloxacillin for secondary infection, no NSAIDs in chickenpox, and the school exclusion rules.

steps.r: There is no specific antiviral for measles: **paracetamol, fluids and rest**.

steps.lead: Yusuf gets **paracetamol** for fever, fluids for dehydration, and **chlorphenamine** if itch troubles him.

steps.title: Which exanthem needs what
nodes: Hand, foot and mouth: symptomatic, 7–10 days

steps.lead: Yusuf's measles needs no antibiotic, but if a classmate has **scarlet fever** they need **phenoxymethylpenicillin**; an infected rash needs **flucloxacillin**.

visual.title: Days from rash onset: when Yusuf can return to nursery
visual.label: Yusuf day 1
visual.caption: Measles is infectious from about 4 days before to 4 days after rash onset (UKHSA).

steps.lead: Yusuf's measles is **notified** to UKHSA and managed using NICE CKS; exclusion follows **UKHSA** school guidance.

steps.text: Prevention is the **MMR** vaccine (two doses). Yusuf's unvaccinated status is the biggest clue in a measles stem.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why measles causes secondary infections, why parvovirus causes aplastic crisis, why rubella harms the fetus, and how hand, foot and mouth spreads.

steps.lead: Yusuf's rash comes from the virus and his immune response to it; scarlet fever's rash comes from a **streptococcal erythrogenic exotoxin**.
Yusuf's **lymphopenia** shows measles' transient immune suppression, which let bacteria cause his **otitis media** and risk pneumonia.

steps.title: Why measles kills through other infections

points: Two weeks later, sister Aaliyah (sickle cell) is pale and exhausted.
She had **bright red cheeks** a few days ago.

steps.lead: Aaliyah caught **parvovirus B19**, which shut down her **erythroid progenitors**. Her sickle red cells already die early, so Hb crashes: **aplastic crisis**.

visual.title: Aaliyah's aplastic crisis
visual.caption: Reticulocytes vanish first, then Hb falls; recovery shows a reticulocyte surge.

steps.lead: Aaliyah's classmates did not need protecting once her cheeks were red: by the time the **slapped cheek** rash appears, she is no longer infectious.
Yusuf's mum is **9 weeks pregnant**. Had this been **rubella**, first-trimester infection could cause **congenital rubella syndrome**.
If Yusuf's nursery has a hand, foot and mouth outbreak, it spreads **faecal-orally** and by droplets, so handwashing after nappy changes matters.

steps.q: Which cell does parvovirus B19 target?
steps.r: Parvovirus B19 infects **erythroid progenitors** in the bone marrow, halting red cell production.

mcq.q: Which virus causes erythema infectiosum (fifth disease)?
mcq.r: **Parvovirus B19**: slapped cheek, then lacy reticular rash.

o: White spots on the buccal mucosa
mcq.r: **White buccal spots** in the measles prodrome.
**HHV-6**: 3 days of high fever, then rash as the fever settles.

mcq.q: What is the most common complication of measles?
mcq.r: **Otitis media** is commonest; pneumonia is the commonest cause of death.

mcq.q: Which is the classic complication of roseola infantum?
How are most viral exanthems diagnosed?
What is first-line treatment for scarlet fever?
When can a child with scarlet fever return to school?
Which drug treats secondary bacterial infection of an exanthem?
How does hand, foot and mouth disease spread?

prompts.q: What is a viral exanthem and how does it usually present?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: fever first, then rash, in a child with a contact.

points.p: Widespread rash caused by viral infection, most common in children
points.why: Scarlet fever is the bacterial exception.

points.p: Systemic viral symptoms: fever, malaise, URTI symptoms
points.why: The prodrome is part of the diagnosis.

points.p: Fever followed by widespread maculopapular rash, often on face or trunk
points.why: Timing of rash relative to fever is key.

points.p: Recent viral illness or infected contact
points.why: The stem often mentions a classmate.

prompts.q: What is the classic presentation of measles?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the three Cs and Koplik spots.

points.p: Prodrome of cough, coryza and conjunctivitis
Koplik spots: white spots on the buccal mucosa
Rash spreads down from behind the ears, days 3 to 6
points.why: Unvaccinated child is the stem's other clue.

prompts.q: Describe slapped cheek, scarlet fever and roseola, with their causes.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one signature sign each.

points.p: Erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19): slapped cheek, then lacy reticular rash
Scarlet fever (Strep. pyogenes): sandpaper rash on torso, strawberry tongue
Roseola infantum (HHV-6): 3 days high fever, rash on day 4 as fever settles

prompts.q: Describe hand, foot and mouth, chickenpox and dengue rashes.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: where are the vesicles, and what does the rash look like?

points.p: Hand, foot and mouth (Coxsackievirus A16): well-demarcated vesicles with red halo on palms, soles, mouth
Chickenpox: generalised vesicles evolving to pustules, mainly torso and face
Dengue: 'white islands in a sea of red'

prompts.q: Name the key complication of measles, rubella, mumps, parvovirus, roseola and chickenpox.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one complication per virus.

points.p: Measles: otitis media commonest; pneumonia commonest cause of death
Rubella: small joint arthritis
Mumps: orchitis, deafness
Parvovirus B19: aplastic crisis in haemolytic conditions
Roseola: febrile convulsions (10 to 15%)
Chickenpox: secondary bacterial infection, necrotising fasciitis risk

prompts.q: How is a viral exanthem diagnosed, and when is testing needed?

points.p: Clinical diagnosis: fever plus rash plus associated features
If severe: blood tests and viral PCR to confirm the organism
points.why: Measles is notifiable and is usually confirmed.

prompts.q: What is the general treatment of a viral exanthem?

points.p: Paracetamol for fever and discomfort
Hydration and rest
points.why: Dehydration is a common reason for admission.

points.p: Oral antihistamine (chlorphenamine) for itch
points.why: Calamine is also used in chickenpox.

points.p: Secondary bacterial infection: flucloxacillin
points.why: Covers Staph and Strep in skin.

prompts.q: How are chickenpox, scarlet fever and hand, foot and mouth specifically managed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: drug, distractor and school rule for each.

points.p: Chickenpox: calamine and paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs
Chickenpox: exclude until all lesions crusted
Scarlet fever: phenoxymethylpenicillin; back to school 24 hours after starting
Hand, foot and mouth: symptomatic only, resolves in 7 to 10 days

prompts.q: How do exanthems cause rashes, and why does measles lead to pneumonia?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: three rash mechanisms, one immune effect.

points.p: Direct viral invasion of skin
points.why: For example HFMD and chickenpox vesicles.

points.p: Immune-mediated hypersensitivity to viral antigens
Toxin-mediated: streptococcal erythrogenic exotoxin in scarlet fever
Measles causes transient immune suppression, so secondary bacterial infection

prompts.q: Why does parvovirus cause aplastic crisis, why is rubella dangerous in pregnancy, and how does HFMD spread?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: target cell, timing, route.

points.p: Parvovirus B19 targets erythroid progenitor cells
points.why: Dangerous with short red cell survival (sickle cell).

points.p: Slapped cheek rash appears after the infectious period
Rubella crosses the placenta and disrupts organogenesis in the first trimester
HFMD spreads faecal-orally and by droplets
points.why: Replicates in gut and skin epithelium.

glossary.exanthem: A widespread skin rash that comes with a systemic, usually viral, infection.
glossary.maculopapular: A rash with both flat (macules) and raised (papules) red spots.
glossary.Koplik spots: Tiny white spots on the inside of the cheeks in early measles.
glossary.coryza: Runny, blocked nose from inflamed nasal lining.
glossary.buccal mucosa: The lining of the inside of the cheeks.
glossary.measles: Highly contagious paramyxovirus infection with the 3 Cs, Koplik spots and a descending rash.
glossary.MMR: Combined live vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella, given in two doses.
glossary.erythema infectiosum: Fifth disease: parvovirus B19 infection with slapped cheeks then a lacy rash.
glossary.slapped cheek: Bright red cheeks of parvovirus B19 infection.
glossary.parvovirus B19: Small DNA virus that infects red cell precursors; causes slapped cheek syndrome.
glossary.aplastic crisis: Sudden halt in red cell production causing a rapid fall in haemoglobin.
glossary.reticulocytes: Young red cells; a low count shows the marrow is not producing.
glossary.erythroid progenitor cells: Bone marrow cells that mature into red blood cells.
glossary.sickle cell disease: Inherited haemoglobin disorder with short-lived red cells, so marrow shutdown is dangerous.
glossary.scarlet fever: Group A Strep infection with a sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue.
glossary.strawberry tongue: Bright red tongue with prominent papillae in scarlet fever.
glossary.erythrogenic exotoxin: Streptococcal toxin that causes the scarlet fever rash.
glossary.Streptococcus pyogenes: Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus; causes scarlet fever and tonsillitis.
glossary.phenoxymethylpenicillin: Penicillin V, an oral penicillin used first-line for scarlet fever.
glossary.roseola infantum: HHV-6 infection in infants: high fever for 3 days, then rash as fever settles.
glossary.HHV-6: Human herpesvirus 6, the cause of roseola infantum.
glossary.febrile convulsions: Seizures triggered by fever in young children.
glossary.hand, foot and mouth: Coxsackie A16 infection with vesicles on palms, soles and mouth.
glossary.Coxsackievirus A16: Enterovirus causing hand, foot and mouth disease.
glossary.faecal-oral: Spread by swallowing traces of infected faeces, usually on hands.
glossary.dengue fever: Mosquito-borne viral fever with a 'white islands in a sea of red' rash.
glossary.rubella: German measles; mild in children but causes congenital rubella syndrome in early pregnancy.
glossary.congenital rubella syndrome: Fetal damage from first-trimester rubella: deafness, cataracts and heart defects.
glossary.organogenesis: Formation of the organs in the first trimester.
glossary.mumps: Paramyxovirus infection causing parotitis; complications include orchitis and deafness.
glossary.otitis media: Middle ear infection; the commonest complication of measles.
glossary.chlorphenamine: Sedating oral antihistamine used for itch.
glossary.calamine lotion: Soothing lotion used for chickenpox itch.
glossary.notifiable: A disease that doctors must legally report to public health (UKHSA).
glossary.UKHSA: UK Health Security Agency, which sets exclusion and notification rules.
glossary.PCR: Polymerase chain reaction, a test detecting viral genetic material.

technique.stem: A 2 year old girl has a 2 day history of fever and is refusing to eat. There are painful ulcers in her mouth and small, well-demarcated vesicles with a red halo on her palms and the soles of her feet. Several children at her nursery have had a similar illness.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis of fever with a vesicular rash in a toddler.

clues: well-demarcated vesicles with a red halo
palms and the soles of her feet
steps.x: Vesicles in a **mouth, palms, soles** distribution in a nursery outbreak.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hand, foot and mouth disease** (Coxsackie A16).

elim: Chickenpox vesicles are mainly on the torso and face, not palms and soles.
Impetigo is honey-crusted, without mouth ulcers or fever.
Measles is maculopapular with the 3 Cs and Koplik spots.
Scarlet fever is a sandpaper rash with a strawberry tongue.

steps.x: **B. Hand, foot and mouth disease.** Palms, soles, mouth.

technique.stem: A 6 year old boy has had a mild cold for a week. Yesterday his cheeks became bright red, and today a lacy, net-like rash has appeared on his arms and trunk. He is well and playing. His mother asks whether a test is needed.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

steps.x: Which test, if any, for a classic rash in a well child?
**Slapped cheek** then **lacy reticular** rash in a well child: erythema infectiosum.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Exanthems are **clinical** diagnoses; no test.

elim: FBC is only needed if aplastic crisis is suspected (haemolytic disease, pallor).
PCR is reserved for severe illness or pregnant contacts.
Biopsy is never needed for a typical exanthem.
A throat swab looks for Strep, not parvovirus.

steps.x: **A. Clinical diagnosis.** Test only if severe.

technique.stem: A 4 year old unvaccinated girl has measles diagnosed clinically. She has fever, cough and a maculopapular rash. She is drinking and passing urine normally. Her temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 130 bpm, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Her chest is clear and ears are normal.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?

steps.x: Management of uncomplicated measles.

clues: chest is clear and ears are normal
steps.x: Well hydrated, no hypoxia, **no complications**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Supportive care**: paracetamol, fluids, rest (and notify).

elim: Aciclovir treats herpesviruses (VZV, HSV), not measles.
No bacterial complication such as otitis media or pneumonia yet.
Penicillin V is for scarlet fever.
Steroids have no role in measles.

steps.x: **C. Paracetamol, fluids and rest.** Viral exanthem = supportive.

technique.stem: A 10 year old boy with hereditary spherocytosis is pale and tired 1 week after his brother had a slapped cheek rash. His haemoglobin has fallen from 105 g/L to 58 g/L and his reticulocyte count is very low.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his anaemia?
o: Direct infection of erythroid progenitor cells
Immune haemolysis of mature red cells

steps.x: A mechanism: why has the Hb fallen?
Haemolytic disease, **parvovirus B19** contact, **marrow shut down** (low reticulocytes).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Parvovirus B19 infects **erythroid progenitors**, so red cell production stops: aplastic crisis.

elim: Platelets are not the problem here.
Splenic pooling gives a high reticulocyte count and a big spleen.
Haemolysis raises reticulocytes; here they are low.
Iron deficiency develops over months, not a week.

steps.x: **B. Direct infection of erythroid progenitor cells.** Low reticulocytes = production failure.

practice.stem: A 2 year old boy who has not received any vaccinations has a 4 day history of fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes. A blotchy red rash started behind his ears today and is spreading to his face. There are small white spots on his buccal mucosa. His temperature is 39.5°C and pulse rate 146 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Cough, coryza and conjunctivitis with Koplik spots and a rash spreading down from behind the ears in an unvaccinated child is measles.

steps.x: Diagnosis of fever and rash in a toddler.

clues: cough, runny nose and red eyes
small white spots on his buccal mucosa
steps.x: Unvaccinated, the **3 Cs**, **Koplik spots**, rash from behind the ears.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Measles.**

elim: Kawasaki needs 5 days of fever with cracked lips, swollen hands and lymph nodes; no Koplik spots.
Roseola's rash appears as the fever settles.
Rubella is milder, with occipital nodes and no Koplik spots.
Scarlet fever has a sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue.

steps.x: **B. Measles.** 3 Cs + Koplik spots.

practice.stem: A 7 year old girl has had a mild cold for several days. She now has bright red cheeks, and a day later a lacy, reticular rash on her arms and trunk. She is well and eating normally.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Slapped cheeks followed by a lacy reticular rash on the limbs and trunk is erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) from parvovirus B19.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a facial then limb rash.
**Slapped cheek**, then **lacy** rash, well child.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Erythema infectiosum** (parvovirus B19).

elim: Impetigo is honey-crusted, around the nose and mouth.
Measles has the 3 Cs and a descending maculopapular rash.
Rubella gives a fine pink rash and occipital nodes, not slapped cheeks.
Scarlet fever gives a sandpaper rash, flushed face with circumoral pallor and strawberry tongue.

steps.x: **A. Erythema infectiosum.** Slapped cheek.

practice.stem: A 13 month old boy has had a high fever for 3 days but has been feeding reasonably well. This morning his fever settled and a pink, non-itchy maculopapular rash appeared on his trunk. His temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and he is alert and playful.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Three days of high fever in a child aged 6 months to 2 years, with a rash appearing as the fever settles, is roseola infantum (HHV-6).

steps.x: Diagnosis of rash after fever in an infant.

clues: fever settled and a pink, non-itchy maculopapular rash appeared
steps.x: Right age, **3 days fever**, **rash as fever goes**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Roseola infantum** (HHV-6).

elim: Slapped cheek starts on the face, in older children.
HFMD gives vesicles on palms, soles and mouth.
In measles the rash comes at the peak of fever with the 3 Cs.
Scarlet fever has a sore throat, sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue.

steps.x: **D. Roseola infantum.** Rash when the fever breaks.

practice.stem: A 5 year old girl has a 2 day history of sore throat, fever and headache. She has a rough, sandpaper-like red rash over her trunk, flushed cheeks and a bright red tongue with prominent papillae. Her tonsils are enlarged with exudate.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: A sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue with exudative tonsillitis is scarlet fever, caused by Group A Strep (Streptococcus pyogenes) via erythrogenic exotoxin.

steps.x: It asks for the organism behind the rash.

clues: bright red tongue with prominent papillae
steps.x: **Sandpaper rash**, **strawberry tongue**, tonsillitis: scarlet fever.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Streptococcus pyogenes** (Group A Strep).

elim: Coxsackie A16 causes hand, foot and mouth.
HHV-6 causes roseola.
Measles has the 3 Cs and Koplik spots.
Parvovirus causes slapped cheek.

steps.x: **E. Streptococcus pyogenes.** Strawberry tongue = scarlet fever.

practice.stem: A 3 year old unvaccinated boy is recovering from measles diagnosed 5 days ago. He now has a new fever and is crying and pulling at his right ear, with yellow discharge from the ear canal. His temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 138 bpm, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. His chest is clear.
practice.q: Which is the most likely complication?
practice.e: Otitis media is the most common complication of measles, due to transient immune suppression; pneumonia is the commonest cause of death but his chest is clear.

steps.x: A complication of measles.

clues: yellow discharge from the ear canal
steps.x: Ear pain and discharge after measles; chest clear.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Otitis media**, measles' commonest complication.

elim: Encephalitis causes drowsiness, seizures or confusion.
Mastoiditis gives swelling and tenderness behind the ear with the pinna pushed forward.
His chest is clear and saturations are normal.
SSPE appears years later with behaviour change and myoclonus.

steps.x: **C. Otitis media.** Commonest measles complication.

practice.stem: A 9 year old girl with sickle cell disease has a 3 day history of increasing tiredness and breathlessness. Her younger brother had bright red cheeks last week. She is pale; her spleen is not palpable. Her pulse rate is 132 bpm and BP 98/58 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
practice.e: Parvovirus B19 (slapped cheek in her brother) infects erythroid progenitors; with short-lived sickle cells, Hb falls fast: aplastic crisis. The non-palpable spleen and near-normal bilirubin argue against sequestration and hyperhaemolysis.

steps.x: The cause of a sudden Hb drop in sickle cell.
Haemolytic disease, a **slapped cheek** contact, no big spleen.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis.**

elim: Splenic sequestration causes a rapidly enlarging spleen.
Hyperhaemolysis follows transfusion, with a high bilirubin.
Iron deficiency develops slowly over months.
Vaso-occlusive crisis presents with severe pain, not pallor alone.

steps.x: **D. Parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis.**

practice.stem: An 18 month old unvaccinated girl with suspected measles is admitted because she is drowsy and dehydrated. Public health needs the diagnosis confirmed. Her temperature is 40.0°C, pulse rate 168 bpm, respiratory rate 44 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the causative organism?
practice.e: In a severely unwell child, viral PCR (throat swab or oral fluid) confirms the causative virus; measles is notifiable.

steps.x: A test to confirm the organism in a severe exanthem.
**Severe** illness and confirmation needed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Viral PCR.**

elim: ASO titre tests for recent Strep infection.
Blood culture detects bacteria, not measles.
A CXR looks for pneumonia but does not identify the virus.
Bacterial throat culture will not grow measles.

steps.x: **E. Viral PCR.** Severe = confirm with PCR.

practice.stem: A 7 year old boy with sickle cell disease is pale and lethargic. His sister had slapped cheek syndrome a week ago. His spleen is not enlarged.
practice.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on blood tests?
practice.e: Parvovirus B19 halts erythroid progenitors, so the reticulocyte count is very low (aplastic crisis), unlike haemolysis or sequestration where it is high.

steps.x: Which result fits the cause of his anaemia?
Parvovirus B19 contact in a haemolytic disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Marrow shutdown: **low reticulocytes**.

elim: Eosinophilia suggests allergy or parasites.
A high count suggests haemolysis or sequestration, with a working marrow.
Platelets are normal in the labs.
Neutrophilia points to bacterial infection.

steps.x: **D. Low reticulocyte count.** Parvovirus stops production.

practice.stem: A 6 year old boy has a 1 day history of sore throat and fever, with a fine sandpaper-like rash on his trunk and a strawberry tongue. He has no drug allergies. His temperature is 38.6°C and pulse rate 120 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Scarlet fever is treated with phenoxymethylpenicillin; the child can return to school 24 hours after starting antibiotics.

steps.x: Treatment of a rash with sore throat.
**Scarlet fever**, not penicillin-allergic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Phenoxymethylpenicillin.**

elim: Aciclovir is for VZV or HSV.
Antihistamine alone does not treat Strep.
Flucloxacillin is for secondary staphylococcal skin infection.
Scarlet fever is bacterial and needs antibiotics.

steps.x: **E. Phenoxymethylpenicillin.** Back to school after 24 hours.

practice.stem: A 3 year old girl has a 2 day history of mild fever, mouth ulcers and vesicles on her palms and soles. She is drinking well. Her mother asks what treatment is needed and whether she must stay off nursery for two weeks.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Hand, foot and mouth disease is self-limiting and resolves in 7 to 10 days; treatment is symptomatic only.

steps.x: Management of a vesicular rash in a toddler.

clues: vesicles on her palms and soles
steps.x: **Hand, foot and mouth**, well hydrated.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Symptomatic care**; resolves in 7 to 10 days.

elim: Aciclovir does not treat Coxsackievirus.
No prolonged exclusion is needed while she is well.
No bacterial infection to treat.
Steroid cream has no role.

steps.x: **D. Paracetamol, fluids and reassurance.**

practice.stem: A 4 year old boy has had chickenpox for 5 days. Several lesions on his arm have become red, swollen and covered in yellow crust, with surrounding erythema. He has no drug allergies. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
practice.e: Secondary bacterial infection of an exanthem is treated with flucloxacillin; NSAIDs such as ibuprofen are avoided in chickenpox.

steps.x: Treatment of an infected rash.
**Secondary bacterial infection** of chickenpox lesions.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Flucloxacillin.**

elim: Aciclovir treats the virus, not the bacterial infection.
Calamine does not treat infection.
NSAIDs raise the risk of necrotising fasciitis.
Penicillin V lacks reliable Staph cover.

steps.x: **C. Flucloxacillin.**

practice.stem: An 8 year old girl has bright red cheeks and a lacy rash on her arms. Her school asks whether she must stay at home to protect other pupils. She is well.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation for why exclusion is unnecessary?
o: All classmates are vaccinated against it
Spread is only by blood transfusion
The rash appears after the infectious period has passed
practice.e: In erythema infectiosum the rash is immune-mediated and appears after the viraemic, infectious period has passed, so exclusion does not prevent spread.

steps.x: A mechanism: why no exclusion?
**Erythema infectiosum** (parvovirus B19).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The rash comes **after** the viraemic, infectious phase.

elim: There is no routine parvovirus vaccine.
Parvovirus spreads mainly by respiratory droplets.
Faecal-oral spread describes hand, foot and mouth.
Adults can be infected; it is a risk in pregnancy.

steps.x: **D. The rash appears after the infectious period.**
